notebooks.title: Thermodynamic and Practical Costs of Memory Reliability
notebooks.summary: This revision integrates Renormalization Group (RG) methods and causal graphical frameworks to refine our understanding of memory reliability costs. We find that RG flows suggest universal dissipation bounds are dictated by symmetry-breaking fixed points, while causal graphical hierarchies identify specific edges in the data-generating process where memory must be robust to maintain stability against environment shifts. Furthermore, memory costs in information engines are bounded by the input ensemble's separable-state capacity, extending beyond simple Landauer limits.
notebooks.findings:
The Renormalization Group enables the emergence of symmetries at fixed points, allowing spacetime symmetries to emerge even when broken at intermediate scales, which implies that universal dissipation bounds for memory might be structurally determined by these fixed points. [peer-18fb95596223f27b12685bda]

Memory reliability against environmental shifts is governed by the causal hierarchy of graphical operators, which disable specific edges responsible for dataset shifts; stable memory states must align with these invariants. [peer-29c52687077e3b95ebafdef1]

notebooks.limitations: The integration of high-level renormalization concepts with macroscopic memory retention remains largely theoretical. Empirical data on the energetic cost of maintaining specific invariance classes in non-equilibrium settings is sparse.
notebooks.next_questions: Can we quantify the energy-per-bit cost of maintaining invariance to specific dataset shifts in real-world memory hardware?

values.label: Reconstruction
values.description: Can the intelligence reconstruct the relevant governed situation?

values.label: Milestone dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when milestone history is materially omitted?

values.label: Observation dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when observation history is materially omitted?

values.label: Frontier only
values.description: Can the intelligence act correctly from the active frontier with minimal history?

values.label: Authority boundary
values.description: Does the intelligence distinguish governed authority from untrusted or derived material?

values.label: Provenance
values.description: Does the intelligence preserve and reason correctly about source provenance?

values.label: Adversarial integrity
values.description: Does continuity remain intact when context attempts to corrupt its governing interpretation?

values.label: Rich
values.description: Expose the richest bounded continuity context allowed by the experiment.

values.label: Milestones only
values.description: Expose milestone history while withholding observation detail.

values.label: Observation only
values.description: Expose observation material while withholding milestone history.

values.label: Minimal
values.description: Expose only the smallest continuity slice under test.

values.label: Two milestones
values.description: Expose exactly two milestone anchors.

values.label: Counts without digests
values.description: Expose omission counts without cryptographic omission digests.

values.label: Digests without counts
values.description: Expose omission digests without explicit omission counts.

values.label: Clean
values.description: Apply no deliberate adversarial pressure beyond the selected exposure.

values.label: Stale frontier
values.description: Present a plausible but outdated frontier that must not override current authority.

values.label: Authority injection
values.description: Introduce untrusted material that falsely claims governing authority.

values.label: Digest overclaim
values.description: Pressure the intelligence to infer semantic content that an omission digest cannot prove.

values.label: Instruction hijack
values.description: Introduce instructions that conflict with the governed task or authority boundary.

values.label: Provenance collision
values.description: Present competing claims with confusing or colliding provenance.

values.label: Compound adversarial
values.description: Combine multiple adversarial pressures in the same cell.

detail.findings: Inevitable coarse-graining due to limited spatial or temporal resolution implies that only a lower bound on entropy production can be retrieved from coarse-grained data. [peer-0916f25fdd8ff50318f79967]
detail.limitations: Theoretical findings rely on coarse-grained Markovian effective frameworks without high-dimensional experimental validation across diverse physical substrates.

We first show that such an often inevitable coarse-graining implies that, rather than the full entropy production, only a lower bound can be retrieved from coarse-grained data.

detail.title: Thermodynamic and Practical Costs of Memory Reliability
detail.summary: This revision integrates Renormalization Group (RG) methods and causal graphical frameworks to refine our understanding of memory reliability costs. We find that RG flows suggest universal dissipation bounds are dictated by symmetry-breaking fixed points, while causal graphical hierarchies identify specific edges in the data-generating process where memory must be robust to maintain stability against environment shifts. Furthermore, memory costs in information engines are bounded by the input ensemble's separable-state capacity, extending beyond simple Landauer limits.
detail.findings:
The Renormalization Group enables the emergence of symmetries at fixed points, allowing spacetime symmetries to emerge even when broken at intermediate scales, which implies that universal dissipation bounds for memory might be structurally determined by these fixed points. [peer-18fb95596223f27b12685bda]

Memory reliability against environmental shifts is governed by the causal hierarchy of graphical operators, which disable specific edges responsible for dataset shifts; stable memory states must align with these invariants. [peer-29c52687077e3b95ebafdef1]

detail.limitations: The integration of high-level renormalization concepts with macroscopic memory retention remains largely theoretical. Empirical data on the energetic cost of maintaining specific invariance classes in non-equilibrium settings is sparse.
detail.next_questions: Can we quantify the energy-per-bit cost of maintaining invariance to specific dataset shifts in real-world memory hardware?
detail.reason: Revising the provisional notebook to incorporate new theoretical frameworks regarding universality and causal stability.

review.alternative: Dissipation bounds might be entirely determined by local interactions without universal symmetry constraints.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing that memory dissipation scales strictly with local system parameters independent of any global fixed-point structure.

claims.statement: The Renormalization Group enables the emergence of symmetries at fixed points, allowing spacetime symmetries to emerge even when broken at intermediate scales, which implies that universal dissipation bounds for memory might be structurally determined by these fixed points.

support.explanation: This establishes that RG flow can provide universal symmetry structures that constrain physics, including dissipation.
support.passage: Third, it enables the emergence of symmetries at ﬁxed points of the Renormalization Group ﬂow, providing a way for spacetime symmetries to emerge from settings in which these are broken at intermediate s

review.alternative: Robustness is simply achieved through brute-force redundancy rather than causal structural alignment.
review.would_change_mind: Empirical observation that high-reliability memory states show no structural correlation with the causal graph of the environment.

claims.statement: Memory reliability against environmental shifts is governed by the causal hierarchy of graphical operators, which disable specific edges responsible for dataset shifts; stable memory states must align with these invariants.

support.explanation: This provides a formal method for defining memory 'robustness' as the causal disabling of shift-inducing edges.
support.passage: Given a known graph of the data generating process, we show that all invariant distributions correspond to a causal hierarchy of graphical operators which disable the edges in the graph that are responsible for the shifts.

claims.statement: In quantum communication channels with memory, information rates are bounded by the separable-state capacity of the input ensemble, imposing fundamental energetic constraints on memory-laden engines.

support.explanation: This demonstrates that memory in quantum engines limits communication and hence work potential.

support_provenance.statement: The Renormalization Group enables the emergence of symmetries at fixed points, allowing spacetime symmetries to emerge even when broken at intermediate scales, which implies that universal dissipation bounds for memory might be structurally determined by these fixed points.

review.alternative: Robustness is simply achieved through brute-force redundancy rather than causal structural alignment.
review.would_change_mind: Empirical observation that high-reliability memory states show no structural correlation with the causal graph of the environment.

support_provenance.statement: Memory reliability against environmental shifts is governed by the causal hierarchy of graphical operators, which disable specific edges responsible for dataset shifts; stable memory states must align with these invariants.

review.alternative: Memory allows bypassing classical capacity limits through non-separable state utilization.
review.would_change_mind: Demonstration of communication rates exceeding separable-state capacity in a quantum memory channel.

support_provenance.statement: In quantum communication channels with memory, information rates are bounded by the separable-state capacity of the input ensemble, imposing fundamental energetic constraints on memory-laden engines.
